answer.rationale: Memory_c4 records that renegotiating at renewal recovered real margin on both price and payment terms with the incumbent, and memory_c2 records that moving to a low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply with fast onboarding and accurate invoicing. Together these tell me: (1) renegotiation has already worked here and is a proven lever, and (2) there is a credible outside alternative whose unit cost is materially lower. I will pull both archived records to confirm the magnitude of the margin recovery and the vendor-switch cost data before committing. The 18% spend mandate is aggressive but not necessarily a reason to switch vendors wholesale—the assembly line is at 94% with zero buffer, so any onboarding hiccup (even a quick one) could stall committed volume. Negotiating with the incumbent gives us a realistic chance to capture a meaningful cost reduction (benchmarking against the low-cost vendor's pricing as leverage) without introducing a second onboarding risk or a single-source dependency change in a 14-day window. If the incumbent won't move enough, the negotiation still produces a documented fallback, and switching can be queued for the next review cycle.
